title: AI Can Help You Write and Produce—But Can't Solve Finding Your Audience
dek: This Emmy-winning screenwriter breaks content creation into three stages: ideation, production, and reaching audiences. AI excels at the first two, but there is no working infrastructure yet to get one thousand viewers willing to pay you monthly.
why: For creators wanting to use AI for writing or content work. If you only care about AI efficiency techniques, this episode is more anecdotal and experience-focused.
who: Independent screenwriters, content creators, and anyone making fiction with AI who fears it sounding AI-generated.
skip: The opening 12 minutes covering career background has low information density and can be skipped.

points.h: What an accidental Tumblr taught him about audience
points.body: While running Best Week Ever, Fred opened a Tumblr just for internal production notes and discovered 10,000 to 15,000 people watching. The accident revealed a core truth: ‘opening your work to the audience is your lifeline.’ This insight shaped every career move since—from TV producer to Twitter's head of content, each step brought him closer to his audience.

points.h: AI is a writers' room, not a ghostwriter
points.body: Fred's method for writers using AI: first, write a ‘who I am’ document with your influences and taste; second, write a ‘what I'm making’ document, even if vague. Then ask AI three questions: does this idea fit this persona, is there an audience for it, where do they gather? The AI doesn't write for you—it functions as a multi-faceted writers' room, helping you think through an idea.

points.h: Creation splits into three stages where AI handles the first two well
points.body: Fred breaks the workflow into ideation/architecture (producing scripts), production (pre-production through final cut—his AI-animated series uses a writing team, animation studios in India, and engineers in Zurich), and reaching audiences (marketing and distribution). Hollywood's marketing teams already use AI to rewrite trailers hourly based on ticket-purchase data. Scorsese using AI to generate storyboards shows where the workflow meets resistance.

points.h: Tools are universal; craft is rare
points.body: Against fears of ‘AI slop,’ Fred points to a lesson from Annie Leibovitz: everyone now carries a camera better than the one she used for thirty years, yet few shoot like her. Tools spreading never means everyone produces quality. The difference lies in depth of self-knowledge before you begin—knowing who you are and what you make—and AI cannot substitute for that work.

points.h: Empty yourself for a day before touching AI
points.body: Fred's practice: before opening any AI tool, spend a day or two handwriting or dictating everything you know about this project. His reasoning is stark—once you open AI, you lose the chance at purity, at something that belongs entirely to you. This ‘emptying yourself’ step is the easiest to skip and the most critical in the entire creative pipeline.

points.h: Claude learned to think like him after hundreds of exchanges
points.body: Working with Compound Writing and Claude Code, Fred iterated on ideas through dozens of exchanges. Claude then independently proposed a series like Brooklyn Coffee Shop but starring 60- to 70-year-olds running a nursing home's Facebook account—complete with audience analysis, production plan, and market fit for the 55+ Facebook-active demographic. Fred felt Claude had absorbed his taste through their long collaboration.

points.h: Success is knowing what your audience wants before they know
points.body: When asked his core principle, Fred says success is ‘knowing what your audience wants before they themselves know it.’ AI can surface relevant material, but it cannot produce the odd personal quirks that make characters alive—the way Homer Simpson's voice actor ad-libbed a single word that made the character work. That only comes from real humans in a real writers' room, not from models.

points.h: A deliberately unforgiving Claude agent keeps him accountable
points.body: Fred's daily workflow lives inside Claude: he feeds it a folder of old work and repeatedly tests whether an idea feels like him, has real audiences, and fits real platforms. He built a Claude agent as his ‘morning accountability officer’ and made it deliberately difficult—if he pivots to a new idea at night, the agent grills him the next morning about abandoning yesterday's thread. At the polish stage, he uses the Pixar ‘because/therefore’ framework, runs it through ChatGPT (which he describes as ‘having read every textbook and seen everything but understanding nothing’), then feeds it into NotebookLM to hear it as a podcast.

quotes.text: Sometimes you look at something and you just go, I want in. And for me, growing up, I grew up on the south side of Chicago, and I watched way too much television. And all I thought to myself is, I want to be on the other side of that screen. I want in.
Annie Leibovitz once said, everybody has a camera that's better than the camera that I used for 30 years in their pocket. But there are very, very few people who are taking pictures like I take.

You have to start with uniquely you, what you know, spend a day or two dumping everything you know about what you're going to do onto a page, right? Do it by hand, do it by whisper, do it by whatever, but empty out. You will never have that opportunity again once you open AI.
So the truism is success is knowing what the audience wants before the audience knows it.
Don't. To me, that's the whole story.
